#4133. Community: "I Think Of Her Every Time I Play It" - Your Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Memories

With the Switch 2 remake of the N64's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time fast approaching, we recently asked Nintendo Life readers to share their memories of the 1998 original.

Whether you were a Zelda veteran taking your first steps into a 3D Hyrule or this was your very first encounter with the series, this particular entry holds an extra special place in many a player's heart, having a profound effect and eliciting emotions that have stuck with us ever since.

So, for those looking to reminisce as we await the new version, as well as Ocarina newbies and younger gamers who, perhaps, are wondering what all the fuss is about, here's a selection of the messages you sent...

Thank you to everyone who took the time to share these moments. Some entries have been edited for brevity and clarity.

Ocarina of Time is what introduced me to one of my best and longest-time friends. I picked up a used copy in the 6th grade, and got stuck navigating the Lost Woods. I was talking to someone about it on the bus ride home from school, and my (now) friend overheard me, and immediately jumped over and gave me advice. After I thanked him the following day, he let me borrow his strategy guide in case I got stuck again. That experience and the long-term friendship it resulted in cements this as not just my favorite Zelda game, but one of my favorite games of all time. Broosh

I was still at college when Ocarina of Time came out in the UK, and I clearly remember playing it religiously on my N64 each afternoon or evening after lessons, over about a three week period. Ocarina totally dominated my life for that brief period, and I genuinely felt like I'd lost a friend when I finally finished the main quest - all these years later I can still recall the hollow feeling of not knowing what would fill the void it left! Still one of the most memorable adventures I've ever had. Tom Charnock

Fighting Dark Link for the first time triggered something in me, as a kid it opened my mind to question who Dark Link was. Was Link capable of being evil? Another core memory I have is the first time I ever beat Ganon I quickly rushed to the phone and dialed my best friend and excitedly told him what I just accomplished. We used to switch turns when it came to playing Single Player games. And who can forget the TITLE SCREEN. Arkay

Not sure why this one sticks out, but in the Shadow Temple, fighting two Stalfos on the ghost ship made me feel like a badass. I was 10 at the time, admittedly. Mattock1987

I do remember one funny occasion where, I turned the N64 to mess around a bit later at night, when I was not supposed to, and went to the title screen, I pressed some buttons and somehow deleted my father's save. I didn't even realize I did so, I just thought it was cool there was keyboard where I could insert my name. Once he went to play the next time, he grounded me for 1 month. It was the first time I was grounded as well. Brandon Silva

My older neighbor had OoT when it came out, and I would go to his house to watch him play. We'd sometimes take turns, until we got to the well dungeon! I remember thinking it was such a scary, grown-up game. I got my own copy when our local Blockbuster rental store closed, and was barely brave enough for the Shadow Temple then. I love the variety of ambiences in Hyrule, and I hope the remake can convey how scary the original could be! Jake

Countdown Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Dungeon Crawl #7 - Grave Expectations

In a collective save played by every kid at my after school babysitter, my only contributions were earning the cow in the horse race with Ingo and the golden scale in the fishing minigame, which taught me the value of learning to take on the weird tasks in any group project. Zach

Playing it when it first came out in 1998, the beginning area felt impressive in the early days of games in three dimensions. But when I left the Kokiri Forest and stepped out on to Hyrule Field, I set the controller down and just sat there in awe. My kid-brain couldn't comprehend how vast a video game could be, and it was beautiful to stare at as the sun slowly set. To this day, each time I replay OoT, I always take a moment to relive that sight. I'm looking forward to being stunned again. Adam Hollerud

My brother and I used to play Ocarina of Time together in the early 2000s. We browsed the early fansites, especially those that documented known glitches. Replicating these glitches ourselves was endlessly entertaining. This was the era when rumors ran rampant and the idea of finding the Triforce didn't seem so far-fetched. Does anyone remember "turning all the gossip stones blue?" The doctored photo of the "Temple of Light?" This game reminds me of my brother and of the unique online culture that surrounded it. Mike DeCou

When both my grandparents were still alive, I used to spend a lot of time at their house, an apartment in a 17th-century building. Going there was an adventure in itself: a big entrance door, three flights of old stone stairs, the smell of soot, and finally, the front door to their big apartment. It was December, and from the very first day, everything felt like a prelude to the long-awaited Christmas Eve. My sister, my cousins and I couldn’t wait to spend some time together. My cousin had a Nintendo 64. I still loved my SNES, but I also had a PlayStation and was really into PC gaming. And 1998 was the year of Ocarina of Time. He owned the game, and I distinctly remember how jealous I was, how I felt almost like a traitor for not owning a Nintendo 64, after being a Nintendo kid for so long. He pushed the cartridge into the console, switched it on, and my world stopped. All of a sudden, I forgot about Doom, Quake, Duke Nukem 3D and whatever else I was playing at the time. I was home. It was Zelda. Matteo Guarino

I was in first grade when we got Ocarina. My mom played it mostly, but I loved watching. One time in school, I was trying to draw the item subscreen (yeah...) and couldn't remember what was in a certain spot. My classmate who was watching and had no idea what it even was suggested "I think you should put a giraffe there". My other classmate slapped me in the face when I told him about the different temples, because "Only God could have those" (church and temple being the same word in Hungarian). Krisi

I played Ocarina of Time so many times that I gave myself a challenge: beat the game with only the 3 hearts you start with, and I did it! (I’ve pictures to prove it) Joseph R Casper

As a 53 year-old, I didn’t get into playing non-sports games until the mid 2000s. Up until then, I was only using my PS2 to play FIFA and Gran Turismo. But my brother who’s four years my junior? He had every Nintendo console. Including the N64. In January and February of 1999, we lost our mum and dad very suddenly. They were only 47 and 51 respectively and it hit us very hard. At the time, I was already married and had our first daughter, but I went to my mum’s place to see my brother every day and I vividly remember one day just sitting there watching him playing Ocarina of Time. It looked utterly incredible and that memory, no matter the brevity, was fundamental in me migrating to Nintendo and playing all the big, proper games. The Zelda’s, the Mario’s, the Metroid’s. That probably isn’t what you guys at NL are looking for here, but for me, just watching Ocarina was huge. It absolutely helped the both of us escape the pain of bereavement, even if only for an hour or two. And, to us, that was priceless. The_Pixel_King

In 7th grade, The Legend of Zelda OOT was my entire personality! We couldn’t afford it when it first released, but in 2001, my parents surprised us with it. I was obsessed! I carried that beautiful N64 instruction manual around like it was my Bible, to school and everywhere I went, studying every page. Some of my favorite memories were sitting with my mom, trying to solve puzzles together, getting stuck, and celebrating when we figured them out. Looking back, it wasn’t just a video game. It was pure magic, a piece of my childhood I’ll treasure forever. Giodannie Isabel de leon

I cried when Link left the Kokiri Forest with Saria standing alone on the bridge in the Lost Woods and again with Mido expressing remorse over how he treated Link before allowing me passage into the Forest Temple. I sobbed when Navi left Link in the Temple of Time. I also [remember] feeling tears of joy after finishing the game and seeing all the lives Link had interacted with throughout my entire journey. I also sobbed when I beat Majora’s Mask and Wind Waker and seeing all the people I had helped and bettered their lives in the process! VirtualVisage87

Sitting before the big TV in the playroom, my friend Maysen and I gazing up at a wide open field, enchanting music beckoning us away to the time of castles and kingdoms and brave knights. Navigating a tricky gated area in the field, feeling so smart. Exploring a quaint village (with a spooky-at-night graveyard). Sneaking about a castle courtyard. Finding a fun yellow mask, at last being allowed to pass the gatekeeper. Then it gets hard! Now, I sometimes revisit this land, experiencing again the faraway, magical places. Imagining my dear friend sitting beside me. Brian

This game is one of my favorite early memories with my mom. I started playing before I could read very well at all. My mom would sit with me and read the dialogue, stories, and signs to me. She would help me solve the puzzles when I was frustrated or didn’t understand some of the lore specific words that were being used. It is one of my absolute favorite memories of growing up and I think of her every time I play it or see the Triforce tattoo on my leg. Thank you Nintendo for all of these awesome memories. Joseph McKinnon

I was already a Zelda super-fan years previously, and when news started coming out for "Zelda 64" my friends and I followed that religiously. So when the OoT release was finally coming, we decided to have a launch party at my house. A couple of us saved and pre-ordered the game at the same EB Games to make sure we all got the gold carts. Immediately after school, Mom picked us up, brought us to get our copies and picked up pizza on the way home. When we all got to my place, starting up that game was awe inspiring. The music, the graphics, everything sucked into Hyrule and enthralled from the start. We all took turns playing while others chowed down on pizza and eventually my mom came out with a cake for us that she had decorated with the Triforce! We played till all hours of the night. It's a vivid and cherished gaming memory for me even 30 years later. David Hannah

I got the 3DS remake in 2019 (I was late) after hearing that it considered the greatest game of all time. I dabbled in the franchise before. I played BotW, and while I love that game, my nine year old brain was used to Mario platformers. OoT was a better introduction with its smaller world. Despite that, I sucked at the game. I loved what I played, it was so cinematic, but when I got stuck on a puzzle, I'd give up and wouldn't come back in months. Thus, I finally beat the game earlier this year. (Yay). The_Mario_Bro

My brother got a cool Christmas gift from the U.S.—an N64 and Ocarina of Time. Even though he wasn’t really into gaming, I totally got hooked! I kept getting stuck and even used the library’s internet to find tips. I skipped school a few times and picked up magazines to help out. I’m not sure exactly how long it took, but I’d guess about a month. Alejandro A

I got Ocarina when it was first released on N64. I had hit a roadblock at the Water Temple. After watching me fail repeatedly, my sister brought me and my game to her friend who showed me exactly what to do. The solution was so simple I was so mad at myself. Then I panicked as he kept playing, so I made up something “we forgot to do” and had to leave immediately. Needing help, the victory was bittersweet. Joshua Younis

I remember before the game came out, there was a hype website with a flash game that taught you the correct path through the lost woods. My friends were all amazed when I just ran through without any trouble. Justin V

I was always a gamer, and so I had made friends with the Best Buy associate. When Ocarina of Time was about to release I went to Best Buy every day in my car until he told me it was in stock, and standing by for release. The night before release I went, and he sold me a copy. Gold cartridge. The night before it came out. I got home at 9pm, my sophomore year of high school and I locked in. I stayed up all night. One of the first people to ever play the game. One of the best gaming memories of my life. Ed Tilden

We're around halfway through these golden recollections - turn the page for tales of young love, final battles, tears, realisations, Sharpies, and uncondonable launch-day activities that are surely past the statute of limitations...

Gavin first wrote for Nintendo Life in 2018 before joining the site full-time the following year, rising through the ranks to become Editor. He can currently be found squashed beneath a Switch backlog the size of Normandy.

These are all lovely recollections. My main memory from my first play through of OoT is "Hey, Listen!".Little punk fairy!

I hate this embargo secrecy. Just tell me when it lifts...

@Broch83 From what I’ve seen, the embargo date hasn’t been officially confirmed, but it’s apparently expected to be lifted around midday tomorrow, November 4.

@MrAnderson16 Well noon tomorrow CET is 1 hour before the New Zealand release, so I guess that must be the latest 🙂

@Broch83 Ah. Yeah, I guess I should’ve included that I’m in the US. Sorry about that.

Always love to hear such experiences from not only familiar names, but also and even more so those who usually don't comment here on Nintendo Life - haven't submitted mine just because I've already shared them multiple times in the comments (for those curious here's the Link to the latest one)!

Aha, didn't expect my tale of the day I beat Ocarine of Time to make it in but here we are. Cheers!

These were great reads! And thanks NL for posting my story as well!

Man, these are so heartfelt! 😭 I’m crying just reading them.

Between this and the Direct last month, I can’t imagine I’ll make it through the game without crying a bunch, lol. Such a special experience, even though I’ve never actually played the original. (Just like hearing Dragon Roost Island in Rito Village for the first time in BotW).

I remember getting stuck playing it and having to call the Nintendo games helpline. Wild to think what is now a simple search engine search used to be a process of calling up a helpline, speaking to a person and trying to describe to them where I was stuck (child link, getting to the third temple).

That and playing the fishing minigame with my dad — we spent hours on that & when I accidentally found the illegal lure I was over the moon (had no idea it excited and found purely by chance from the fact I played the fishing game constantly).

@MrAnderson16 Ok. I am now 97% certain it will be 6 am EST tomorrow. Both because that fits with the release time in the earliest eShop territory. Also because 1 outlet posted their review at 6 am EST today, and now took it down, so I assume they messed up and were a day early.

Must’ve not got that many if you included mine! 😆

Thank you for allowing me to read all these sweet memories.

in the end this game has etched its way into the memories of almost everyone who played it. And that is worth more than any metacritic

My sister and I received Ocarina of time for Christmas and the guidebook. I was only 7 years old, my sister 11. I was the map man, giving her instructions and advice. She handed me the controller for boss fights as I was better at those. We beat ocarina of time multiple times like this. I preordered a copy for me and her. Can’t wait for her kids to experience it for the first time and make their own memories.

Ocarina of Time was the first game I ever played. I was probably 4 years old and NOT allowed to play video games. I was at my aunt's house and my 18 year old cousin asked me, "do you like video games?" Then brought me upstairs, turned on LOZ OOT, handed me the controller and just left the room. I was in castle town and I ran around for like an hour having no idea what to do but I know I thought it was fun. This is probably one of my ealiest memories of anything!

Glad to see my comment made it through! Loved reading everyone's as well.

I was a PS1 kid at this time. So over winter break one of my friends was going to be out of town for 2 weeks and he let me borrow his N64 and OoT so I could experience this game I was hearing so much about.

I had to devour the game so I could finish it before the 2 week deadline was up, but boy was it a good time!! Cold snowy days, no school, no homework, just immersed in Hyrule.

I ran into that friend ~25 years later and told him how grateful I was that he let me experience that. After all, lending someone a console was a big deal back in the day! An amazing show of trust! lol

#4132. Xbox Black Friday Sale 2026 Leaks Early, Thousands Of Games Set To Be Included

We're still a little while away from Black Friday in late November, but Xbox is already preparing for a massive Black Friday sale in a few weeks' time, and the list of potential games has leaked online in recent days.

This is courtesy of a user named "Bloomy" over on the CheapAssGamer website, who says there are specifically 3,519 items in the list. The actual number of discounts is set to be lower than that though, as Bloomy breaks down each "Deluxe Edition" and similar bundles into individual items (some of which aren't purchasable on their own).

There's every chance the list could change between now and November 19th, which is seemingly the start date, but as things stand, the likes of 007 First Light, Ace Combat 8, Star Wars: Zero Company, The Blood of Dawnwalker and Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced look set to receive discounts as part of the sale.

We initially came across this via a post over on the official Xbox subreddit:

This certainly lines up with what we'd expect from the Xbox Black Friday Sale - last year's one began on November 20th (which, like this year's reported date, was also a Thursday) and included over 2000 games.

It's worth keeping in mind that Xbox may start providing discounts for accessories and potentially even consoles (you never know!) before the game-focused sale begins on the 19th, so keep an eye out for those as well.

Naturally, you'll be able to find all the Xbox Black Friday 2026 game deals and their prices on Pure Xbox as soon as the sale begins in mid-November, but you might need to bear with us as it's set to begin on the release date for GTA 6!

#4131. Arkane survival negotiations reportedly seeing "several forms of takeover" considered ahead of November deadline, as Marvel's Blade production nears end

217 jobs are on the line at the studio, report claims

Update: A Microsoft rep has told PC Gamer that the company have "extended the consultation period by one additional month as we explore options, including finding a partner to support [Arkane] through the development work still ahead." "This is a defined extension," they added, "and we remain committed to keeping the Works Council informed throughout the process."

So, Microsoft's consultation with Arkane's Social and Economic Committee now looks set to roll on until December 13th. Though, as we previously noted, the Printemps Écologique union have said that this consultation deadline isn't the deadline by which Arkane need to have found a buyer, with the setting of the latter deadline being one of the things that needs to take place as part of the ongoing negotiations.

Negotiations over the future of Dishonored and Deathloop developers Arkane Lyon are reportedly seeing "several forms of takeover" considered as a November deadline looms for the divorce Xbox set in motion back in July. French law makes the process of shuttering or chucking away studios a lot harder for companies like Microsoft than it is elsewhere in the world, hence Arkane's fate still being up in the air while production work on Marvel's Blade nears completion according to the report.

French publication Le Monde are behind this paywalled report on how the negotiations between the two sides are going. They note that due to a French law brought in as of 2014, companies with more than 1000 staff have to search for a buyer for three months before they can throw up their hands and shut up shop. In the case of Arkane Lyon, the report says 217 jobs are at risk.

The deadline for these consultations with Arkane's Social and Economic Committee (via Gematsu) is November 13th, though Arkane have longer than that to pin down a buyer for the studio - speaking to RPS, a Printemps Écologique union representative clarified that the exact date is being negotiated and subject to change.

The Le Monde report also cites a representative of Printemps Écologique, who along with the Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Video (STJV) union seemingly aren't too happy with Microsoft's attitude throughout the process so far.

Microsoft have told Le Monde that they're "actively seeking a partner to support the next phase of development and enable the commercialisation of the [Marvel’s Blade] project". According to a union rep cited in the report, the superhero game is "nearing the end" of production, with the unions understandably backing Arkane's work and hoping that it will see the light of day.

Xbox wrote as part of an announcement of layoffs in September - the second of multiple waves in a mass chopping that still isn't over as of writing - that they expected consultation over how Arkane will move forward "to continue through the end of the year".

Solidarity to all of the developers at Arkane and here's hoping these negotiations do end with a result that keeps the maximum amount of them in work and making the games they want to make.

This article has been updated to clarify that the deadline for Arkane finding a buyer isn't the same as the deadline for the consultation period.

Remake had a bigger job – setting up what would follow

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy lead Naoki Hamaguchi may be working towards what's shaping up to be the biggest and boldest installment yet, the grand finale of Revelation, but it turns out that, of the three, the first game was the hardest to make.

In an interview with French content creator mistermv, translated by Genki on Twitter (and verified by GamesRadar+), Hamaguchi is asked what the biggest development challenge of the trilogy has been, and he immediately points back to where it all began.

For a start, the development team was much smaller in the beginning. At first, Hamaguchi notes, the team was only comprised of 30 people – a number obviously eclipsed by the final credits on the game.

But more than that, Remake also had the challenge of setting up what would follow it. The start of the project meant deciding on the entire visual look and graphical quality for the Remake trilogy, for example, all while working to the pressure of pleasing the many massive FF7 fans, with the worry of the devs' efforts being insufficient in meeting players' lofty expectations.

On the other hand, Rebirth and Revelation were able to follow in the footsteps of the foundation built by Remake – while they may have been larger and more ambitious, as Hamaguchi puts it, they had a base to go on, and the team working on them had grown and evolved, too.

Hamaguchi and other FF leads have previously spoken about how creating the Final Fantasy 7 remake in the trilogy format has allowed the devs to take on feedback between installments, too, hopefully making each experience better than the last for players. For example, Hamaguchi is aware that many players felt that Rebirth had an overwhelming amount of content, and while Revelation "probably" has even more, the devs have made some key differences in signposting what side-content will earn you what rewards, and ultimately making it easier for players to decide what they care about pursuing.

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation has a hard mode you can select from the start, Naoki Hamaguchi says, but it "won't function in the exact same way as it did in Remake and Rebirth."

#4129. Sony Wants You to Trade In Your PS5 for $400 if You're Not Using It

Sony is sending out notifications to PS5 players in the US, encouraging them to trade-in their console for cash if they’re not using it.

The programme – which runs through a third-party named Back Market – promises up to $400 for a base PS5 console with two DualSense controllers, depending on their overall condition.

Microsoft recently sent out a similar email to Xbox Series X|S customers, encouraging them to offload any consoles they’re not currently playing.

Here’s a look at Sony’s message, courtesy of ResetEra:

Well, we’re in unprecedented times, and the price of new consoles has rocketed.

Moreover, the memory crisis has dramatically reduced stock – it’s quite difficult to get a PS5 Pro these days, even if standard systems may still be readily available.

But the real reason is there’s no money in a dormant device.

If someone buys a second-hand console, there’s a good chance they’ll purchase GTA 6 through the PS Store and a PS Plus subscription – that’s potential cash in Sony’s pocket which it wouldn’t have earned if the console sat in a storage unit gathering dust.

It is really strange to see console manufacturers promoting trade-ins like this, and of course they’d rather you use your system everyday and make purchases within their ecosystem.

But if you’re not, it seems companies want you to offload your console, so someone else can pick them up and hopefully spend some money.

#4128. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Switch 2 Cast Features A Returning Voice Actor From The N64 Original

Nintendo has today shared even more insights into the development of Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 in the latest chapters of its Ask the Developer series. One such story is all about the new voice cast, which apparently features some familiar pipes.

Series Producer Eiji Aonuma and game Director HokWai Ng explain that the team didn't want to "mess with established perceptions of how certain characters sound based on the original," so Nintendo conducted blind auditions to really focus on matching the voice to the role.

"We deliberately hid the voice actors’ names during the Japanese auditions to force ourselves to decide based solely on which voices most closely resembled those of the original," Aonuma-san explains.

As luck would have it, such an approach led Nintendo to select an actor who had previously appeared in the N64 original — voicing the same character, no less! "None of us saw that coming," Aonuma-san notes.

In true Nintendo hush-hush fashion, the interview doesn't mention the voice actor or character by name, but there is already a fair amount of speculation out there that Kaori Mizuhashi (the actor who voiced Navi in the original) might be returning to voice the fairy again this time around.

We won't know for sure until we get to play the game ourselves — and even then, we have to imagine that Mizuhashi would only be handling the Japanese version — but what a neat little bit of luck on Nintendo's part. Hey, you're unlikely to find anyone who sounds more like the N64 original.

The first two chapters of this Ask the Developer series revealed the remake's development team and some design sketches alongside a bunch of other interesting info. You can read more about the highlights in our coverage below.

#4127. Woim is the earth-guzzling, self-bisecting sokoban pick-me-up I needed after a week of games industry disasters

While ladling city-builders into the Maw's feeding trough this week, I remarked that being a worm must really suck. Then came the closure of BioWare, layoffs across other EA studios, further depressing genAI revelations, allegations of antisemitism at indie gaming events, a big Capcom data breach, and yet more worrying tidyings about Arkane.

I rescind my earlier observation: I would like to be a worm. A happy little worm, tunnelling after golden apples in the moist and forgiving earth, where there are no emails or press releases at all. The only thing I have to worry about down here is my butt growing so big I get stuck behind it. And also getting chopped in half by sliding doors, but it turns out this may actually help with the first problem. See for yourself - video below.

Ah, to be a soil-dwelling invertebrate in Woim, a puzzle game with a touch of the sokobans, consisting of 50 levels and an unspecified quantity of secrets, scattered across four subterranean worlds. The idea in each level is to crawl around a grid layout to reach a golden apple, opening the exit.

As with non-videogame worms, this involves a certain amount of ingesting earth and pooping it out behind you, but you can't just devour the whole layout. You'll need to guzzle red apples that make you longer, so that you can (for example) keep pressing a switch with your body as you slither towards a door. Or you might have to shove a rock onto that switch. Or shove that rock onto a water jet to propel it somewhere you can't reach.

Later on, there are breakable eggs that must be carried to nests, daisies that push back outward when you take your weight off them, scissors with which to snip yourself into separately functioning halves, and hats. I don't think this is an entirely accurate worm simulator. As in sokoban, the major problem is trapping yourself, but you can undo moves without penalty by tapping Z.

I've played six levels, and it's a jolly production. The music wobbles and boobles along, and your worm has a habit of looking at you expectantly when you get stuck that makes me giggle. Read more about it on Steam. If, unlike me, you've had a really uplifting week and are in sore need of a sokobanlike charged with maximum ontological dread, may I recommend Void Stranger.

#4126. Former Xbox Manager Explains Why $500M Cost For Gears: E-Day Doesn't Tell The Whole Story

Update [Mon 2nd Nov 2026, 1pm]: Windows Central's Jez Corden has weighed in with a few extra details this morning as well, explaining that according to a "variety of trusted sources", The Coalition has been contributing to many other Xbox projects over the past 6-7 years.

All of these seemingly factor into the $500M budget that has been attributed, although it's unknown to what extent.

"...The Coalition worked for over a year and a half on a prototype project for Xbox that Windows Central understands was ultimately canceled. The Coalition also worked on Avowed, Hellblade 2, Clockwork Revolution, State of Decay 3, Grounded and Grounded 2, and has even contributed to the upcoming StarCraft reboot."

"The Coalition also spent a great deal of time working with Epic Games on the "Matrix Awakens" Unreal Engine demonstration, as well as the Alpha Point demo, both of which were intended to showcase the potential of UE5 on next-gen consoles and PCs."

Nevertheless, Corden warns that $500 million is a "lot of money to invest without a specific structure in place to explain why some of these costs were worthwhile to Microsoft auditors", and that there have even been "some internal disagreements over how exactly attribution should be distributed".

Original Story: Over the past couple of weeks, there's been a lot of chatter about a rumoured $500 million cost for The Coalition to make Gears of War: E-Day, alongside debates about how much of that money went on the game itself.

Speaking on the weekend, former Xbox exec Derek Reese shared his take on the situation, suggesting that The Coalition is heavily involved with supporting Microsoft's branch of the Unreal Engine, which is where a lot of the cost goes.

Here's what the ex-Senior Product Manager of Xbox Game Services had to say:

So much of that cost is The Coalition being on the hook for the Microsoft branch of Unreal and one of the flagship titles. I should know, I tried to get leadership to support a plan to have other studios adopt it and write off the support costs. Same problem with Turn10 and ForzaTech.

This aligns with what Jez Corden of Windows Central was saying a few weeks ago as well, who originally suggested that because The Coalition is "the technological glue for all of Xbox", some of that money is "spread across the entire portfolio" and even goes towards The Coalition's help on other Xbox games like Fable and Forza Horizon.

Corden confirmed yesterday that Reese's comments align with what he's heard:

In some follow-up posts, Reese mentioned that he thinks The Coalition "accomplished their end goals very well and delivered a great accomplishment in E-Day", while also suggesting that there's a "publicly visible pattern of allowing departments to shoulder the costs of leadership direction", pointing to Double Fine as a recent notable example.

So, hopefully we can put this one to bed now! It seems the $500 million budget IS a legit figure for Gears of War: E-Day, but it's hard to realistically attribute that entire figure to the game itself.

The big question is what Xbox thinks about all of this, including whether the game has been a success in terms of sales, Premium Upgrade conversions, Xbox Game Pass subscriptions and its pulling power as an Xbox console exclusive, and it could be some time until we know the answer to that.

News Rumours Persist That Xbox Spent $500 Million On Gears Of War: E-Day, Despite Some Objections

E-Day exceeded expectations and made me fall in love with the series even more

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

ANY well managed corporation has a time management system where employees and contractors register their time and what project they were working on. Even if they are salaried employees that don’t get paid by the hour. This is used not only to track personal time off and/or sick time but also precisely to manage independent project budgets.

It can sometimes be annoying as an employee that works full time in a single project (as those employees might see it as pointless), but it’s vital for management to know what projects (not teams) are eating up money.

#4125. Matt Reeves teased the Two-Face actor's true identity in The Batman 2 months ago, and nobody noticed

Matt Reeves might have teased a different actor playing Two-Face from the start

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Batman 2 director Matt Reeves might have already given away that another actor was playing Two-Face – and nobody noticed.

Thanks to a behind-the-scenes look at Heidi Klum's latest Halloween costume, it was seemingly revealed that Sebastian Stan will not be playing Two-Face in the upcoming DC sequel. Instead, Brian Tyree Henry looks to be the actor bringing the iconic villain to life, and Stan is instead playing Victor Zsasz.

When Reeves confirmed Henry's casting on Twitter, he captioned the post "Welcome to the party, man…"

"Partyman" is the name of Prince's iconic Batman soundtrack song, and the video features him wearing the Joker's makeup on half of his face, with a crowd wearing masks covering half of their faces, too. Could this be a veiled reference to Two-Face, who famously has one half of his face disfigured? It certainly looks like it…

wait https://t.co/3CEFVyrWKKNovember 2, 2026

The leak also seemed to confirm that the Court of Owls will be part of the film, as well as Sebastian Koch's role apparently involving prosthetics.

After Reeves had to step away from production for a personal matter, Steven Soderbergh has taken over to finish principal photography. "I am so happy he's come on to help Matt," star Robert Pattinson told us recently. "It's incredibly generous of him – and he's doing it in the loveliest way. It's completely selfless.

"I think Matt had put so much work into the script, and we're almost done," Pattinson added. "So for someone to come in and say, 'I just want to help Matt do it; I want to do it in conjunction with him and just get it to the edit.' And to have someone who's as talented as Steven doing it is great."

The Batman 2 arrives on February 18, 2028. While you wait, check out our guide to all the upcoming DC movies and TV shows for everything else that's on the way.

#4124. 'The Elder Scrolls 6' Finally Has An Official Title

We forget quite how long we have been waiting for official news from the next entry in Bethesda's The Elder Scrolls series, and now the studio has finally, finally lifted the lid on its title.

As revealed by Todd Howard himself in a new studio 40th anniversary video, the next game in the series is titled The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel (yep, the very same name that was reported last week).

The reveal doesn't come with much more information than that. There's a brief glimpse of a metallic scroll being unearthed from some sand, the title logo, and the following quote from 'Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell', but that's it:

The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate.

That's all we have right now. Still no release date, still no confirmed platforms, still no gameplay. But hey, a name is a good start!

Given Bethesda's support for Switch 2 so far, our fingers are crossed that we'll see the next series entry come our way at some point (whenever that may be), but there's no official word on that front for the moment, unfortunately.

#4123. "This was not a Creative Assembly developed game": Total War boss points the finger at external partner for Shogun 2 Complete Edition disaster

But concedes that "we took our eyes off" its creation

Last week, Creative Assembly and Sega pulled Total War: Shogun 2's remastered Complete Edition from Steam, after an avalanche of complaints about technical problems and some AI-generated art. Now, Total War vice president Roger Collum has written a personal apology, while pinning some of the blame on an unnamed external partner. He's also clarified Creative Assembly's stance on generative AI, conceding that the studio do use it to help with "analysis, debugging, or speedy prototyping", but that they're against using it to generate game assets and art.

"I get many of you are angry and disappointed about the state of the Shogun 2: Complete Edition release," Collum writes on the official Twar Reddit. "We are too – especially the team members who have put everything into Total War games for years, some even decades. This was not a Creative Assembly developed game. It wasn’t subject to our same internal reviews and quality assurance. We took our eyes off its external development, with all our teams focused on our next big projects. However, whatever the development arrangements, Total War is our franchise and our name is on it."

Again, Collum doesn't name the external developer in question, but Mataboo Games are listed as co-devs on the Steam page. Collum says that SEGA and a small team of senior developers are working with the external team on "next steps", with details to follow. In the meantime, he has some general thoughts on how and when the Twarfolk make use of generative AI tools.

"I want to be very clear on the studio-wide stance on generative AI, because I know there are many questions about where we stand," Collum writes. "We are a craft studio. Our games are made by incredibly talented people, and we do not believe in a world where technology replaces the creativity of humans. At Creative Assembly we do not use generative AI to create game assets, including AI-generated art. We demand the same of any external developers we work with. The situation with Shogun 2: Complete Edition is being investigated."

Collum adds that Creative Assembly do, however, use AI tools for "support" purposes. "It shouldn’t replace the creator," he says. "I don’t believe that AI can replace the human experience, judgement and creativity that awesome experiences come from. Can AI tools help with analysis, debugging, or speedy prototyping so our experts can focus on making incredible games? Absolutely."

Collum ends his message by requesting that people don't abuse individual Total War developers. "Our community teams, QA, designers, and everyone in between are doing their job, as asked by the company," Collum writes. "Their safety is our priority. They do not deserve, and we will not tolerate, harassment or being singled out online and personally criticised." Collum warns that if you're nasty to developers, the studio may need to be less transparent in future.

I'm not sure I wholly buy the argument about "taking our eyes off" the game, given that Creative Assembly and Sega ran a bunch of trailers and marketing for it and sent round a FAQ detailing, among other things, how it would affect mods. While unavailable for purchase, the Complete Edition's Steam page is still live as of writing with "overwhelmingly negative" reviews. Creative Assembly and Sega have reinstated the original game's Steam page while they work on kicking the CE into shape.

#4122. Guide: GTA 6 Release Times and Preload: When Can You Start Playing?

Probably the most anticipated game of all time, GTA 6 is now just a few weeks away. As the launch draws closer, we're covering everything you need to know about its PS5 launch, including preload options and release times. In this GTA 6 guide, we cover the GTA 6 release times and preload.

On this page: GTA 6 Release Times and Preload: When Can You Start Playing?

Rockstar has confirmed GTA 6 will officially be playable from midnight on 19th November in your local time zone. As such, the game will unlock and be available first in New Zealand. If you preload the game, you'll be able to start playing GTA 6 as soon as it hits midnight on 19th November where you live.

If you pre-order the game, GTA 6 will be available to preload from 10th November. This is nine days before the game comes out, and was just brought forward two days by Rockstar.

Pre-ordering digitally means your preload should start automatically on PS5 as soon as it becomes available. The boxed physical version, which is just a code in the box, comes out on 12th November, the same day. You can redeem the code inside the case and start preloading the digital version of GTA 6 if you buy the game this way.

Rockstar has now officially confirmed the GTA 6 file size on PS5, and what you'll need to download, is 212GB. This is one of the biggest downloads and installs on console in history, and will probably only get bigger through patches and the addition of GTA Online.

GTA 6 is available digitally on the PS Store, or in a basic physical version that ships without a disc. The latter provides a code in the box that you redeem on the PS Store to get the digital version.

The two PS5 digital versions on offer are: Standard Edition and Ultimate Edition.

#4121. BioWare staff "should be given the first opportunity and the federal support" to buy the studio and keep it running, says Canadian political party leader

Hope. It's in short supply at the moment. Regardless, I hope that something a Canadian politician's proposed in a post scoring easy likeability points at the expense of EA's recently installed owners comes to pass, no matter how unlikely it is to do so at this point. Rather than being unceremoniuously shuttered, leaving the world staring down the barrel of a future without new games from a storied studio, BioWare should be handed over to its staff with backing from the Canadian government.

Nationalise BioWare, basically. Well, sort of. "The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio," is what Avi Lewis, leader of Canada's New Democratic Party, wrote in a post following the closure. "They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity - and the federal support - to buy it and run it themselves. And if we want to avoid the Mass Effect effect in Canada, we should be keeping private equity out, not welcoming it in."

You can almost hear the horde of suit-wearing money-knowers who've sensed that suggestion's been made and are about to descend from orbit to yell about taxpayers' money being used to help ensure the creation of future adventures starring space blokes who say 'We'll bang, ok?'. I should also point out that since I'm not Canadian, it wouldn't be the country I live in spending some of their cash on helping the Veilguard avoid being veilgone to the depths of the vault where EA keep Burnout and ten million other defunct series people would like to see return.

The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio. They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity - and the federal support - to buy it and run it themselves.

In all seriousness, I'm not totally sure it'd work out in the long run, but it's something. An alternative to a company erasing a studio from existence because the Saudi Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner have been allowed to load them up with a ton of debt rather than reaching further into their own pockets.

So, I say screw it. Set up a new position called Minister for BioWare to ensure the devs have what they need to get their heads down that next Mass Effect which reportedly had a trailer leak the other day. Just make sure it's not some right-wing crank, or BioWare might run into some of the same problems it'd been feared their generally very inclusive games might face under Saudi ownership.

Marvel fans have noticed that the Avengers: Doomsday artwork reveals a key detail about the X-Men storyline

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just over a month before the new MCU movie lands in cinemas, new Avengers: Doomsday artwork has found its way online, but a closer look at the X-Men reveals an interesting detail about Ian McKellen's Magneto.

The images were shared on Twitter by French fansite HexFacility, which has been known to share legit Marvel leaks in the past. Although we cannot confirm that the images have come from Marvel Studios, it looks like the artwork has been taken from Hasbro's Marvel Legends Avengers: Doomsday Series, as many of the images line up with the heroes' action-figure counterparts and the packaging.

The new images give us a new look at Captain America, Thor, Doctor Doom, Yelena Belova, Bucky Barnes, Red Guardian, Sue Storm, Reed Richards, the Thing, M'Baku, Shuri, and more.

The artwork also features X-Men Professor X, Magneto, Gambit, Cyclops, Mystique, Nightcrawler, and Beast. However, one Marvel fan on Reddit has noticed an interesting detail about Magneto. If you take a closer look, you can see that most of the mutants are wearing an X belt to signify they are part of Charles' X-Men squad, including Magneto. Check out the images below.

⬣ AVENGERS: Doomsday - Visuels Promo pour le Professeur Xavier, Magneto, et Nightcrawler ! https://t.co/MAlFKJwENYNovember 2, 2026

"I love how everyone has the X mark on their belts, even Magneto. It shows everyone is on the same side, despite Magneto and Mystique being rivals in the past," said the fan. Although we cannot see the front of Mystique's belt, it looks like she too is sporting the X-Men uniform. In the original Fox-era X-Men trilogy, Charles and Erik were often at odds, with Erik, aka Magneto, often waging war on the human race. But Charles was always there with his mutants to make him see sense.

We already knew that the two would be somewhat civil in the new movie. In the Avengers: Doomsday trailer, we see them sitting together, looking pretty terrified as their universe faces destruction from Doctor Doom. Alongside McKellan and the late Patrick Stewart as Professor X, Doomsday welcomes back original X-Men James Marsden as Cyclops, Rebecca Romijn as Mystique, Alan Cumming as Nightcrawler, and Kelsey Grammer as Beast, and adds Deadpool and Wolverine's Channing Tatum as Gambit.

But Magneto doesn't really have a choice either way, as everyone is going to have to work together if they have any chance of stopping Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom. As the official synopsis reads, "Doomsday is set to bring beloved heroes from three distinct universes together as they’re set on a deadly collision course and face an existential threat unlike anything they’ve ever encountered."

Avengers: Doomsday hits US theaters on December 18, and in UK cinemas on December 16. For more on Marvel Phase 6, check out our guide on how to watch the Marvel movies in order, and keep up with upcoming Marvel movies on the way.

#4118. Future? No Thanks! dev removes AI-generated voices from game and offers refunds to players who feel "betrayed"

Next game will be"completely hand-coded".

Open world ecosatire Future? No Thanks! has been updated to remove some AI-generated voices, after lead developer Paolo "Molleindustria" Pedercini belatedly disclosed his usage of the technology earlier this week. He's also offering to refund people over Paypal or Venmo if they "still feel betrayed" by this.

The update removes two instances of text-to-speech generated voicework for in-game robot characters – an automated toilet and an automated translator in a hair salon. In his previous blog, Pedercini wrote that he used genAI for these characters as a spoof of generative AI. He's decided to replace them with human voice-acting following a number of angry reactions on social media and some coverage in the press.

"The voices were recorded earlier this year but I decided to not use them because I thought the actual uncanny text-to-speech was funnier in that context," Pedercini writes in a new blog post. "Alas, the new generation of text-to-speech counts as user-facing AI-generated content and that keeps creating all sorts of annoyances and bad optics."

Pedercini still thinks the text-to-speech voices belong in Future? No Thanks! "In my opinion the game is worse now, but only, like, 0.001% worse," he observes. In less acrimonious tidings, he's also tweaked the game so that the "various gigs give you a bit more money, possibly preventing some situations of soft-locking players from achieving all the quests."

The blog includes a "personal update" in which Pedercini expounds rather bitterly upon the backlash to the game's genAI elements. "Somebody from Bluesky (the Twitter/X clone) dragged me due to a post disclosing what I foolishly thought a minor use of generative-AI in Future? No Thanks!" he writes. "I gave versions of that statement multiple times before, whenever asked by festivals and events. Steam doesn’t require disclosure of generative AI for things like code assistance so many people assume their favorite indie games don’t use AI at all just because the developers stay mum."

For context, Valve updated Steam's rules in January to allow "efficiency" tools, such as coding assistants. I'm basing this on anecdotes and conversations with other devs, rather than any kind of statistical survey, but it seems very likely that a lot of developers on Steam aren't disclosing their genAI use - the policy has always been more of a gesture on Valve's part than a mechanism of real accountability.

"Not me, I’m a good boy and I wanted a page I could link to that explains that NO, this is not a vibecoded slop game but YES, I did ask chatGPT to fix a broken shader and a few things like that," Pedercini goes on. "More foolishly, I added a paragraph that sounded like I was trying to exculpate myself by poo-pooing on all the colleagues that advocate for an AI-free life." (The paragraph in collection was deleted after the original blog's publication, but not before it had been screengrabbed and shared on the socials.)

"Look, it was not a good post," Pedercini concedes. "Defeatist, hastily written. I thought nobody would read it. Anyway, slow news day, everybody fucking hates AI, the whole scene piled on."

Pedercini proceeds to caricature some of the people yelling at him over social media: "Am I satirizing the puppy killing machine by KILLING PUPPIES?" He compares the anger he's received to being harrassed by Adam Baldwin's followers at the height of the Gamergate hate campaign.

Pedercini ends by sharing a list of developers who've sworn off generative AI. "Big props to them," he writes. "Give them a follow. SteamFest is drowning in actual slop, help them stand out. And I hate to break it to you, but you should probably assume that all the studios that have not made a public statement against all generative AI are using it for coding in some capacity. I’m guessing this episode isn’t going to encourage more voluntary disclosures." As for his next game, it'll be "completely hand-coded".

#4117. "I Had Some Overdue Homework" - Ocarina Of Time Remake Features More Water Temple Tweaks

Yes, Aonuma knows how much you hate those Iron Boots

It's no secret that Eiji Aonuma can see the issues with Ocarina of Time's Water Temple. The series producer spoke about it when the game launched on 3DS, and it continues to haunt him today, as he's brought it up once again in the latest Ask the Developer interview.

"I had some overdue homework: I wanted to do something about the Water Temple I created 28 years ago," Aonuma-san says of the Switch 2 remake. He touches on all the dungeon's much-discussed sticking points (the item menu annoyances, confusing layout, etc.), and confirms that he "had the team make some adjustments in this version".

Director HokWai Ng expands on these changes, stating that the Switch 2 remake has "made item toggling much easier" — it's now mapped to the D-pad, borrowing from the simplicity of the 3DS version — and there have been certain structural tweaks, too: "We also changed some of the walls that made it easy to lose your sense of direction to lattice-style structures, making it possible to see the rooms beyond them and get a better sense of the overall space."

What's interesting is seeing Aonuma-san speak about his intentions behind the dungeon's original design. It always gets so bogged down in negativity that it's nice to get a reminder about where it all came from:

When I designed the Water Temple all those years ago, I wanted to create an experience where simply being underwater was fun. It was a time when there were very few 3D games that even let players go underwater. I enjoy freediving, and what I find fascinating about being underwater is how different everything feels. The sounds change, and it feels like you’re in a completely different space. I wanted to create a place where players could experience those sensations.

Of course, the 3DS version came with its own Water Temple tweaks, including mapping the Iron Boots toggle to the touchscreen and adding directional lines leading to the water level switches on all the walls.

And yet, there are still those of us on Team NL that love the Water Temple in its original form — warts and all. It'll be interesting to see how the Switch 2 version matches up later this week.

#4116. November 2026 PS Plus Essential Games Available to Download Now

Tour a Dead Island, board a Monster Train

Today's the day for Sony's penultimate PS Plus Essential update of 2026, which delivers a further three PS5, PS4 games for members to download and play.

Here's what PlayStation has to offer this month, available to redeem until 1st December 2026:

The games are available now in the UK and across Europe, and availability will reach the USA later in the day.

As long as you add the games to your PSN account and maintain an active membership, you will always have access to the titles — they always remain playable and be tied to your profile. Again, you've got until 1st December 2026 to redeem them to your account.

Dead Island 2 is the standout title, and represents a fantastic open world romp through an undead LA. If you enjoy your time with the game, it's worth noting the Expansion Pass, which provides access to two DLC packs, is on sale right now for just £3.89 / $4.79. You've got until 5th November 2026 to buy it at that price.

I think this is a pretty good selection of PS Plus Essential games, but I'm apparently in the minority. 34% of 3,500+ voters reckon it's a "crap selection" — they're not easily pleased! Only 16% of voters registered a vote to suggest they're pleased with the lineup in our weekend Poll.

Are you happy with what's on offer? Let us know in the comments below.

#4115. Feature: 25 Years Later, How Many Of These Original Xbox Launch Titles Have You Played?

From the original North American launch on November 15, 2001

Welcome to the month of Xbox's 25th anniversary! Xbox will be celebrating that milestone officially on November 15th, but before we get there, we thought we'd use the chance to highlight the very first games that ever launched on Xbox.

To do that, we're going back to the initial list of North American Xbox launch titles, of which there were 20 in all. Some of them are obvious standouts, such as Halo: Combat Evolved, Fuzion Frenzy, Dead or Alive 3 and Project Gotham Racing, while others are more obscure - Arctic Thunder, Dark Summit, Mad Dash Racing, etc.

Here's the full list of all 20 launch titles:

Now, of course, some of these games are still playable to this day on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, while others have always remained locked to the original Xbox. The likes of Project Gotham Racing, Shrek and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2x are highly-requested additions to the Xbox backwards compatibility library, but it seems unlikely they'll ever make the cut at this point - almost certainly due to licensing reasons.

However, you may not know that games like Cel Damage and Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee are still playable to this day on modern consoles, and they're still well worth checking out despite their age.

So, how many of these original Xbox launch titles have you played? Let us know down in the comments section below, and please do give us your recommendations with some of the obscure ones - NHL Hitz is still one of my faves!

Including exclusives & backwards compatible titles

#4114. "Go play GTA 6, we need to detox": Wardogs studio Bulkhead is taking a month-long break

The Wardogs team is planning to take a long break to celebrate the success of its early access release, and CEO Joe Brammer knows that it'll probably be fine because players will have plenty to occupy them – in the form of GTA 6.

Speaking to Edge Magazine, Brammer explains that the team has worked hard to earn the right to play hard. "Everyone has done something that's not in their job description. Everyone wears multiple hats, because they can see the path to success with the product."

With the early access launch of Wardogs in the rear-view, the entirety of developer Bulkhead Studios will be taking an extended break, with leave stretching throughout the entire month of December. It's a bold strategy, but one that Brammer is quick to double-down on.

"We're going to make sure players know they can fuck off in December," he says, suggesting the team does have some idea of the backlog of bug reports and balance complaints that could be waiting for them come January. The hope, clearly, is that those players will be too distracted by something else to be blasting the Bulkhead forums: "Go play GTA 6, we need to detox," Brammer says.

With most games wondering how they'll hope to hold onto their audiences once Rockstar drops its nuke – and Fortnite offering near-unlimited freebies to certain lucky players – it's almost refreshing to see a team unapologetically accepting that its fans will have something else on their minds, and hoping that they'll come back once they're finished with Leonida.

Elsewhere in Edge 430, check out our Grand Theft Auto VI exclusive – The state that never sleeps

#4113. Factorio's final major update has rolled off the assembly line, adding "the things we wanted to do for 2.0 but didn't have time for"

Including QoL tweaks, new visuals, and more predictable asteroids

In one of the happier endings to occur in games this week, impossibly enormous resource management sim Factorio has just released its last-ever major update – version 2.1 – on its stable branch. As previously heads-upped by developers Wube Software, 2.1 doesn’t make any big new additions to its planets or tech trees, but does sneak in more than 30 quality of life improvements and minor new features for both the base game and its Space Age expansion. Including, they say, "the things we wanted to do for 2.0 but didn't have time for." Nice to get a few final pieces out the door before it closes, eh.

There’s also an updated trailer, if you want to watch promotional footage for a game that may well have enveloped your every waking moment since 2016.

Factorio - Trailer 2026 Watch on YouTube

Here are some of those changes I’ve picked out at random. "Mixed rockets: Rockets can now carry multiple different items in one launch, so no more sending a full stack of everything just to build a small platform." Nice! "Land mines can be used as tripwires and enemy detectors." Devious! "Asteroid damage now depends on the asteroid's remaining health instead of its speed, so it is much more predictable." Convenient! Not counting how you’re still being hit by an asteroid. There’s also now the ability to play Space Age without the controversial Quality mechanic, as well as the ability to flip pumpjacks and burner miners instead of merely rotating them, like some loser.

The 2.1 update also gives Factorio one last graphical polish, including a handful of new models and a "new pump rendering system that can connect to fluid wagons no matter how cursed your station is." I’m merely pretending to be a Factorio expert for the purposes of publishing this article, though I will say – from experience building piplines in Deep Rock Galactic – that a series of tubes is only truly cursed if it still works, in spite of itself, at transporting liquids. Otherwise you’ve just got a pile of broken pipes, again, like some loser.

This isn’t the end-end of Factorio, which Wube Software have said will continue to get bug fixes and support-level updates while they largely move on to "other game prototypes/experiments." Though even if it was, it’s had a bloomin' admirable run, starting with four years of early access - successful enough to cement it as the de facto basis for later automation-builders like Satisfactory and Dyson Sphere Program – and continuing to enrapture aspiring industrial managers into the present. Ollie has over 1,000 hours in it. Maybe I’m the loser for making light of it.

#4111. Review: Zero Parades: Director's Cut (Switch 2) - ZA/UM Returns With Another Atmospheric, Cerebral Yet Overly Familiar RPG

How does a studio follow an era-defining masterpiece without the original creative forces behind said masterpiece? The answer, for better or worse, is to emulate the experience almost completely.

ZA/UM emerges from a controversy far too storied to cover here with a follow-up to existential crisis simulator Disco Elysium. Zero Parades is once again about a lone figure of questionable authority and skill, wandering a political melting pot of a city and trying to find salvation or oblivion. It’s achingly beautiful and constantly thought-provoking, but also very familiar for fans of Harry DuBois’ misadventures in Revachol.

The complex and multi-branching story follows Hershel Wilk — whose spy name is the distinctly cooler-sounding CASCADE — as she is reactivated after being put out in the cold following a botched mission. She awakens in her apartment with a hazy memory and her partner, Psuedopod, passed out in a chair. The meat of the story has CASCADE try to find out why her partner is in a comatose state and what exactly the Operant, her shadowy handlers, want her for.

Hershel/CASCADE ventures out into the bustling streets of Portofiro, an ideological morass that struggles and rebels under the watchful eyes of multiple factions. The societal clock has been reset to zero following the Latour-Woolgar Treaty and CASCADE’s handlers work intelligence for the ruling communist power of the Superbloc. Meanwhile, propaganda and word-of-mouth for techno-fascist group La Luz permeates every conversation she has.

ZA/UM doesn’t hold your hand in a narrative sense; the world around you is a complete mystery to the player and in most cases, the protagonist. You are left to glean an emerging plot from colourful NPCs around the city.

Not a traditional mainstream RPG experience by any stretch, the game plays out more like an investigative tabletop adventure. You navigate dialogue trees, while passive and active skill checks determine when and where information becomes available.

There’s a character build system of sorts that gives you relative freedom in what kind of amnesiac spy you wish to be. Yellow skills govern how personable and empathetic you are, pink focus on physical spycraft, and purple are technical aptitudes.

There are three status meters to balance throughout the game: fatigue, delirium, and anxiety. Actions and poor conversation choices have a direct impact on these levels, and maxing them out will force a downgrade of a corresponding colour of skills. These status effects can be managed by successful dialogue rolls, consumables, and several environmental interactions. Keeping one eye on these levels adds a layer of tension to the relatively action-free investigations.

Conditioning offers a further way to boost CASCADE's core skills. Throughout her wandering, our confused spy will discover certain thought patterns that she can condition, which in turn buffs a cluster of her abilities. These thoughts have specific unlock criteria that, much like everything else in the game, are never obvious. Unlocking them, however, adds an element of intrigue and abstract progression to your character build.

Another way to boost certain skills is by assembling an aesthetically ridiculous outfit from items picked across the city. Your skills are also vital in several decision-making encounters that occur throughout the story. These multiple-choice scenarios usually require a series of rolls and give your status levels a beating. Dramatic encounters are the closest the game gets to action and they contrast just enough with the rest of the gameplay to be exciting.

Navigating Portofiro is a smooth experience, falling somewhere between point-and-click-style pixel hunting and free exploration. ZA/UM has made incremental traversal and UI improvements over Disco Elysium that have really paid off. Movement and investigation are intuitive, and exploration is decidedly less laborious than in the previous game. There is still a lot of aimless wandering as you figure out the next objective, but a helpful map and scanning system keeps things moving at a healthy clip.

The city itself is dripping with atmosphere, thanks in no small part to the beautifully haunting score from Fernando Cabrero. The rogues and grotesques that our anti-hero interacts with are as meticulously designed as their dialogue, and the voice acting is superb (though CASCADE's inner monologue can get a bit jarring). It's one of those games where you can't wait to meet the next NPC and engage in a philosophical battle of wills and/or idiotic argument about what it means to be 'cool'.

Yet, as engrossing as this spy-out-in-the-cold odyssey is, returning fans will feel a pervading sense that they've been here before. Those that laud ZA/UM's debut opus may be clamouring for more political events set in a European dystopia, but they won't get much else besides that. Newcomers, on the other hand, are in for an engrossing, at times mind-bending treat and should certainly follow up with the superior predecessor once they're done here.

The Switch 2 version of Zero Parades is jam-packed with new content and native console features. Noteworthy is the inclusion of mouse controls, which work well and are much better suited to environment interaction than the regular controller setup. Alongside mouse controls, touchscreen support, and HD Rumble 2, this Director's Cut version of the game arrives with new outfits, a behind-the-scenes Backstage mode, and a reported 40,000 additional words in the script.

One downside is the 30fps target, which noticeably mars the experience of wandering the populated streets of the city on a large screen. The isometric perspective and UI-heavy gameplay feel much better to play undocked. It just feels baffling that 60fps was not possible, given the hugely demanding games the console can run at that level.

Going some way to balancing out the performance shortcoming is a generous suite of accessibility options, including colour balancing, contrast and dyslexia settings.

Fans who patiently awaited the next game from the Disco Elysium studio can rest easy. Zero Parades is another complex, intelligent and gorgeously presented RPG. It oozes style and boasts an engaging narrative and cast.

That said, it brings nothing new to the groundbreaking experience offered by its predecessor.

#4110. Borderlands Has Sold 100 Million Units Across the Series, and There's a Shift Key to Celebrate

Publisher 2K Games has announced a major sales milestone for its super popular looter shooter series, Borderlands.

The franchise has now sold more than 100 million copies to date, across all platforms and games. It's marked the occasion with this video:

In addition, developer Gearbox is celebrating by giving players 20 Golden Keys in every mainline Borderlands game — that includes Borderlands 1, 2, 3, The Pre-Sequel, and 4. You can claim this bonus with the below Shift Code:

And here's that same Shift Code in plain text for all you copy-paste fans: CZKJJ-35RH6-T9K9C-9TJJT-SXRCT

The Borderlands series began on PS3 back in 2009, and at the time there was nothing quite like it. The combination of its cel-shaded visuals, divisive humour, and co-op looting and shooting made it stand out, and it's been very popular ever since.

Across five main games and numerous spin-offs released over the best part of 20 years, it's now sold over 100 million units — impressive stuff.

There was even a movie, though the less said about that the better.

There aren't many franchises that are in the 100 million+ club, but it joins the likes of Gran Turismo, Dragon Quest, Mortal Kombat, Monster Hunter, Resident Evil, and more.

The latest game, Borderlands 4, recently concluded its first year of post-launch support and DLC. In a blog post addressed to the community, Gearbox says the team is "cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year."

In the meantime, "Weekly Activity refreshes and Community Challenges will continue" and the studio wants to hear what players want moving forward.

#4109. OG Xbox Game 'Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee' Gets Remastered, But What Do The Critics Think?

Was it worth digging the original Xbox title back up?

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee launched on the original Xbox in 2003, a few months after its GameCube debut, and sadly, only in North America. The kaiju arena-brawler, which depicted the iconic King of Monsters, Godzilla, body-slamming Ghidorah into various cityscapes, has apparently made a big enough impact to warrant Atari funding a remaster in 2026.

Sadly, the whole North American release made it quite difficult for us Brits to get our mucky mitts on the game, and DAMM wasn't a big enough deal for Xbox to share the game with the rest of the world. DAMM did get the backward compatibility treatment, however, only on Xbox 360, and again restricted to North America.

I guess then, we're quite pleased Atari decided to take a punt on a DAMM remaster. Even though it seems to share many of the original's downfalls, Godzilla's WWE antics are going to be available on November 3rd on Xbox Series X|S, and best of all, I can play it from my lovely little home in Cornwall.

So, here's what the critics are saying about Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered:

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered brings the classic kaiju brawler roaring back with impressive rebuilt visuals, satisfying arena destruction, and chaotic multiplayer battles. While its limited roster and tedious character unlocks feel dated, the accessible combat and faithful Godzilla presentation make this a thoroughly entertaining return for the King of the Monsters."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered feels like a new game with its graphical upgrade, held back slightly by a lack of any other meaningful new additions and a somewhat grindy gameplay loop."

"Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a satisfyingly faithful update to a beloved Kaiju brawler. It’s simple and fun, with local and online multiplayer keeping you around for the long haul despite a wafer-thin single-player experience. Now if we could just get a remaster of Save The Earth and Unleashed."

Review Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (Switch 2) - The King Returns With A Fun But Thin Kaiju Brawler

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is at its best when it simulates the idea of smashing kaiju toys together as a kid in short sessions with friends, and at its worst when it attempts to prolong a game that never had much depth to begin with. The result is a remaster I’m glad exists considering the drought of Godzilla brawlers, but with a few caveats–not to mention the sting of realizing that the original GameCube and Xbox game were absent of arbitrary grinding."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered remains goofy fun, and Atari’s remaster looks and runs well. It’s still a rather simple game and probably not the most comprehensive when it comes to the characters and lore. But it’s a good time and offers quite a few different modes to get acclimated and beat up famous faces."

"Right now, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a great version of a good retro game. Because the game was remade from the ground up, I wish the developers had made a super version of the Godzilla trilogy with more content. While Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered’s combat is really fun, there’s not much depth. There are lots of modes, and a bit of RPG unlocking, but this isn’t a deep fighting game that’s going to be played at tournaments. It’s a great budget buy for Godzilla fans. But more content would have made Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered a more obvious recommendation. If you’re at all curious, or have any fondness for the original game, it remains a fun time."

"In the media shadow of sacred monsters like Grand Theft Auto VI and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, only an equally fearless monstrosity could face them: Godzilla. Nearly a quarter century after its release on GameCube, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee returns with a remaster that discreetly refreshes the audiovisual experience and improves the progression without betraying its structure. The core is that of a 3D fighting game in which kaiju clashes are accompanied by the destruction of entire cities, in a blaze of explosions and particle effects. Behind this chaos lies a combat system that's immediate, but not always precise and balanced, suspended somewhere between classic fighting games and the festive jumble of a party game. The mechanics are simple, despite a certain unwieldiness in the movements, and the best of the action is found especially in local multiplayer."

Well, there you have it, folks! Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is an almost perfect example of a good '7' rated game. At the time of writing, the remaster is holding down a 72 score on Metacritic.

What's interesting is that the original Xbox release scored 73 on Metacritic - a single point higher than the remaster. It's funny how 23 years can pass and a game can be reviewed almost identically.

Godzilla Minus Zero is about to make a lot of noise

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Godzilla Minus Zero is so loud that one viewer received repeated "loud environment" warnings from their smartwatch throughout a screening of the super-sized sequel.

Posting on X, content creator @imPatrickT shared an image of the 90 decibel warning, along with a simple statement: "Godzilla Minus Zero is the loudest movie I’ve ever heard in my entire life. This will be a reference title for testing theater setups. Unbelievable film, and the definition of FILMED FOR IMAX."

For reference, 90dB is roughly the volume experienced when standing next to a lawnmower, or a subway train, so that's pretty damn loud. Hearing protection is recommended for sustained exposure to sounds over 80dB. Minus Zero is 'only' 135 minutes long, but you might still want to pack earplugs anyway if you have sensitive ears.

It's been a noteworthy year for loud movies, as many questioned if Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey was too loud. This seemed to be a particular concern in IMAX screenings, where volume levels are set by the filmmaker. The Cyclops' scream and the Poseidon storm were the main culprits, with some reporting that the Cyclops' scream hit as high as 120dB in their screenings.

Of course, it makes sense for Godzilla Minus Zero to turn up the noise, as the sequel will see Big G square off against King Ghidorah, though don't expect it to turn into a "giant pro wrestling match" between two kaiju, according to director Takashi Yamazaki. The movie has already proven a big hit with critics, and in our own Godzilla Minus Zero review, we awarded it 4.5*, calling it "easily one of the best films of the year."

As for what's next, the official trailer promised "everything ends here" and "there will not be a third fight," but Yamazaki recently told SFX that he would "probably say yes" if Toho offered him a third film.

Godzilla Minus Zero releases on November 6. For more, check out our guide to all the most exciting upcoming movies for everything else worth seeing this year (and beyond).
