#4107. Mass Effect 3 ending discourse ignored the RPG's scale, ambition, and exuberance, including that of its oddly great co-op

Ah, come on, it was fine. Better than fine. We can argue for another fourteen years about whether BioWare should have redone the ending or not, but Mass Effect 3 was really a compendium of endings, a ludicrously ambitious wrapping-up of dozens of plot threads, character arcs, and running gags. Even if you can point to other RPGs that, on an individual basis, are more branching and reactive, Mass Effect 3's largely successful closing of a galaxy's worth of choose-your-own adventure books - filled in and followed across three evolving instalments - showed an audacity and grandiosity that no other three-part series had matched before. Or, at least on that scale, has pulled off since.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

It didn't hurt that Mass Effect 3 also had the trilogy's fiercest, bangiest action by far, nor some of its highest-stakes, often most lip-chewing moments of decisionmaking. It is true that the accumulation of War Assets wasn't always as heavy on character drama as the game-long preparation for Mass Effect 2's Suicide Mission, but then you don't simply play Mass Effect 3 to make a number go higher. You play it to punch or hug reporters, to love or shoot your friends, to save or damn entire species. And it has loads of that, right up to the point to have to choose the colour of an explosion. Potentially beyond, if you treat the (assuredly, delightfully) fanservice-forward Citadel expansion as Shepard's true last ride.

Back in 2013, and again with 2021's Legendary Edition, I was sad that Mass Effect 3 ended and glad that it happened. That, at the risk of appearing less furious at EA's stewardship than I am, does not change with BioWare's closure. What does bother me is the uncertainty over what now happens to Mass Effect 3's surprisingly entertaining, weirdly long-lived co-op mode.

I don't doubt this was put in for boring, C-suite, "gamers want multiplayer" reasons. But that only gave the resultant palled-up superpower maelstroms a sense that they were better than they had any right to be, with explosive moments of player-to-player power synergies and spacious, blindspot-filled maps that could maintain a thrilling feeling of being permanently surrounded. Post-release additions to the species-spanning character roster also showed glimpses of that same, fuck-it swagger that BioWare exhibited in the campaign, as they increasingly moved away from familiar soldier archtypes towards electric whip wielders, regenerating lizards, teleporting ninjas, and three-foot-tall psychic asthmatics. While many of today's co-op shooters fret over miniscule balance changes, in pursuit of some mythically perfect meta, Mass Effect 3's gave you a crate of action figures and told you to go nuts.

While I haven't played it recently, there's a small but loyal contingent who do, and for their sake I hope the multiplayer's P2P setup helps it survive the EA cull. I was, and for now technically still is, too good to be doomed to oblivion. Or, worse, vibe-coded Legendary Edition mods.

#4106. Countdown: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Dungeon Crawl #8 - High Spirits

With five Sages under my belt, it was time to head off to the final temple in my Ocarina of Time replay to pick up the last of 'em before the big showdown (not technically the 'last', but you catch my drift).

I chose to polish off the Shadow Temple last week, so I was left with no other direction than to head west to the Gerudo Desert and finish the main quest with one of my favourite dungeons in the game.

On the off chance that you're only just joining the series now, I am going to get into some pretty key dungeon spoilers here, so turn back now if you've been saving yourself for the Switch 2 release!

I mentioned last time that I wasn't sure why I always tackled the Shadow Temple first, but as I made my way through the Gerudo Fortress and up to the Colossus, I think the answer might have dawned on me: it's because I always want to finish on this belter.

Much like the Fire Temple earlier in this playthrough, I often forget about the Spirit Temple. Perhaps because it's so late in the game and I'm usually a little sleepy by this point, but I don't know this one like the back of my hand and I can rarely complete it without a good bit of backtracking.

The same was true when I returned to it this time. While I remembered the mid-dungeon time travel and the mirror puzzles, everything else felt new.

I love the way that right from the jump, the temple is split in two: the left side only available to Child Link after talking to Nabooru, and the right to Adult Link once you've got the Silver Gauntlets. There's a great mystery to the whole thing, knowing that you've still got half the dungeon unexplored when you finally learn how to get rid of that big rock in the entrance hall.

But first, Child side! After crawling through the tunnel and swearing to return with the Gerudo treasure, this first half effectively serves as the dungeon's tutorial. The left side is full of rooms with multiple entrances, switch puzzles in the main statue chamber and simple sunlight triggers. I was particularly keen on watching those light puzzles develop this time around, progressing from bombing a wall to trigger a stationary switch, to moving the switch into light, to bending the beam to meet its target. It's classic Nintendo.

I flew through the Child portion, for the most part. Telegraphed attacks aside, the Iron Knuckle fight is a nice change of pace, and I still love the cinematic pause in the middle with Nabooru shouting out before being dragged away by the sisters.

The Adult Link half is where the Spirit Temple really comes into its own, though; it's just satisfying encounter after satisfying encounter. Finally shifting that massive stone that previously barred the right entrance? Satisfying. Seeing the outside of the temple from the other colossus hand to the one where we found the Silver Gauntlets? Satisfying. Being able to do anything at all in the temple's central colossus room after previously floundering around as a child? Immensely satisfying.

It carries through into the puzzles. Almost every dungeon has a central mechanic that develops as you work your way through, but the Spirit Temple takes the biscuit for the breadth of that development. The Mirror Shield is such a wonderful puzzle item. The aim refraction stunned me when I first played through it, and still today, seeing that tiny patch of shield-shaped light move around the wall feels so very modern. Heck, Nintendo reused the very same formula in Tears of the Kingdom's Lightning Temple for a reason.

It caps off with the wonderfully long-winded mirror slalom, bouncing light between multiple rooms to lower a platform into the colossus chamber and then use the light to...melt the statue's face? Nintendo was really cooking with this one.

It even carries through into the boss fight. After one last Iron Knuckle encounter (I had forgotten the plot twist of Nabooru being inside the suit!), it was time to face Twinrova.

I love a puzzle boss, and I think my passion for them might come from this very encounter. Bouncing the fire/ice beams back at the opposite sister is still a little fiddly, and the connect-three elemental dodging of the second phase slows the pacing, but the prioritising of puzzle-solving over timing or mechanical skill is sublime. Give me something like this over a combat-first encounter any day.

Does anyone else feel strangely upset at seeing the haloed sisters ascend off the mortal plane at the end? No? Just me, then.

Honestly, this one rules. Dividing one temple between Child and Adult Link is an inspired choice, and the sunlight puzzles boast some of the best development in the game. I cannot wait to play it all over again with some fancy HDR lighting to really make the beams of light pop.

That's it for the main quest dungeons, but you know I couldn't leave this series without a run through the grand finale. Keep an eye out as I embark on one last dungeon crawl soon!

#4104. I've got egg on my face because Steam's Personal Calendar feature has apparently been a test this whole time and is only now actually a fully fledged component

I'll be honest folks: I didn't know that Steam's Personal Calendar feature was still technically in testing. I've been using it here and there to keep track of what's come out recently or what's coming out imminently, and have generally found it to be fairly reflective of the kinds of games I was interested in. It just worked! Yet lo and behold, a post from Valve went out yesterday announcing that the feature has launched out of Steam Labs "and is considered a full feature of the Steam Store."

The feature, if you've missed it, is "another way to see recommended games for you, showing both recently released and upcoming games filtered down to the set of games we think you are most likely to be interested in," as Valve explain it anyway. "It uses your recently played games to find people with similar playtime profiles to you, and then looks at the games those players have been adding to their wishlist or playing." I do wonder if there's a bit more going under the hood here, as my playtime count is all over the place, with nothing above 50 hours on there, and that's an exception to the norm (I'm from more of a console background, alright).

But even still, my recommendations do remain pretty good, showing me games that I have since added to my wishlist. I'm never opposed to new discovery tools, especially considering how bad Valve can actually be at that kind of thing. Apparently the recommendation system refreshes daily "to incorporate the latest data. In reality you aren't likely to see your recommendations change all that much from day to day, but as time goes by you will obviously see new things pop up as the 8-week horizon of the calendar marches forward, or as games lock in their release dates."

This comes as part of a broader swathe of changes Valve have been introducing to Steam over the past couple of years, including one from last month that will change its homepage discounts and events section to be a bit more algorithm based. Perhaps it's some kind of weird prepwork for that new Half-Life they're almost definitely making but only talk about accidentally.

#4103. 'Too Big A Risk' - Game Developer Sparks Debate After Delaying Playtest Due To AI Concerns

Will it push us towards a more cloud-focused future?

As AI continues to adopt a bigger influence in the gaming industry, there have been concerns in some circles about how people can use AI to reverse-engineer games, including for upcoming titles that haven't even been released yet.

This became a particular talking point a couple of weeks ago when Moonlighter developer Digital Sun Games decided to delay a planned (PC) playtest for their upcoming game ReVamp, worrying that the code might be reverse-engineered before they actually had a chance to release the full game.

Here's what they had to say in a statement at the time:

This ended up sparking a whole bunch of discussion regarding developers that might choose to adopt the same strategy, potentially opening us up to a future where demos and trials for upcoming games will become less prominent.

Some even took it further, suggesting that reverse-engineering will push us to a cloud-focused future:

A few people pushed back in the comments, suggesting that games have still been successful despite the existence of piracy and other elements that have threatened their potential over the years, while others highlighted that stronger protections in the future may be able to limit the damage from reverse-engineering situations.

For what it's worth, it's been reported in recent days that Claude has begun blocking attempts to clone and reverse-engineer games, and it was confirmed by an Anthropic dev that the idea is to "steer it away" from recreating other developers' titles because infringing IP is against the company's usage policy.

Ultimately though, it's too early to know what the future holds, but it's an interesting topic of discussion at the very least. Don't be surprised if instances like this still crop up, and hopefully it's something that Xbox is actively thinking about.

Tips on how to defeat Bai Chilian, Lady of the Twin Serpents in Phantom Blade Zero

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Beating the Phantom Blade Zero Bai Chilian boss fight isn't easy as this serpentine woman moves erratically and quickly, and can deliver some devastating blows. However, as always with these boss fights, knowledge is power, and so is blocking, parrying, and dodging. Learn Bai Chilian's attack patterns and take in the tactics I've laid out below, and the fight will become much easier to manage – just be aware that there's a second phase that mixes things up a bit!

Bai Chilian, Lady of the Twin Serpents, is a story-critical boss, so you can't progress until you've defeated her. Despite her often-rapid movement, she isn't as difficult to bring down as she seems – if you've already beaten the Phantom Blade Zero Three-Faced Puppet, you should have very few problems! With all of that in mind, here are my tips for beating Bai Chilian in Phantom Blade Zero:

Once you've depleted Bai Chilian's health bar, she'll transform into the Sacrificial Serpent for a second boss fight – thankfully there's a checkpoint! Despite having a radically different moveset since she can now swing around using puppet-like strings, much of the same logic and tactics from phase 1 applies, but here are some additional tips:

Once you've beaten both phases of the Bai Chilian fight, you'll get the Broken Illusory Pipa, a crucial story item that's tied to the Phantom Blade Zero Whence The Weeping quest. You'll also get a very good dual-wield weapon, the White Serpent & Crimson Viper swords, and the Resonance Talisman Accessory, which increases your maximum Sha-Chi – both very useful to have for the journey ahead.

This also marks the end of the Crimson Forest region, as you'll be immediately whisked to the next region. Hopefully you've already completed the Phantom Blade Zero A Healer's Mercy quest and answered the Phantom Blade Zero Nimble Thief questions though!

#4101. Paralives' first major update slips to next year, but when it comes you can expect some pretty meaty improvements for all of its main features

Since launch back in May of this year, life sim Paralives appears to have been trucking along nicely, with the dev team offering up fairly regular updates with all sorts of tweaks big and small. Certainly confidence-inspiring for an early access game, especially one as systems-driven as it is. And now, the Paralives team have outlined their plans for the game's first major update, which seem very catered to improving the core experience.

As part of a four point plan they outlined, first up on the docket is "buffing up the basics." This is all about strengthening some of the currently existing Live Mode systems. That means improvements to how relationships function by unlocking more things when a relationship level goes up, adding in more interactions that change your Para's emotions, improving the Community Centre's bundles and tweaking the economy curve so it isn't as easy to get money.

The next point is on expanding the Live Mode, meaning the addition of a pair of new skills, adding in more together and story cards, new relationship label unlockables, and more jobs too. Build Mode will also see some improvements, with a big focus on build breaking bugs. You can also expect new bits of furniture and items, and a tweak to furniture and item efficiency.

Lastly, there are also planned improvements to the Paramaker. One is by adding in more hairstyles and clothing items, notably baggy outfits, and the other is increasing the range of fat and muscle sliders "to represent a wider variety of body shapes." As a bigger person myself I'm always enthused when character creators actually let you have a fat body, so this is a welcome point from the dev team.

Worth noting that this list "is not final," and some things may be pushed back with others getting added in. Also worth noting is that while this first major update was planned for the end of 2026, it's been pushed into next year as the team needs a bit more time. You can read about all of these plans in more detail over on Steam.

#4100. Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds - Year Two 2.0.0 Patch Now Live - New Additions, Changes & Improvements

Update [Wed 4th Nov 2026, 1:15am]: The Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds Year Two Update (Version 2.0.0) has now gone live. It kicks off with the Godzilla Pack, which is the first paid Year Two DLC. Bayonetta also joins the race today as the first free character update of Year Two.

Here's the full rundown from Sega's website:

Duels let you take on other racers in 1-on-1 showdowns. This mode can be played both offline and online. While racing, you'll have an extra ace up your sleeve: Duel Boost. This gauge fills up as time passes and you use items. Once it's full, press the button to boost ahead. Time your Duel Boost well to pull off clutch comebacks!

Face off against CPU CrossOver racers in offline 1-on-1 matches. By defeating these powerful rivals, you'll earn unique rewards. Keep on progressing to unlock the new racer Bayonetta!

Test your skills in a 1-on-1 match against players worldwide. Give it everything you've got in an adrenaline-pumping race where it's just you, your opponent, and the track.

Compete for the most points within a limited number of races. Join these limited-time events and earn Duel Medals. Exchange them for exclusive horns, auras, and other rewards!

Face off against a friend or family member with this Friend Match option. *On Nintendo Switch™ and Nintendo Switch™ 2, you can play this mode in Local Wireless.

The Super Slot amplifies the effects of your Gadgets. *To use the Super Slot, you must first unlock the Grand Master Plate by racing at least 40 times. Players who have already fulfilled these conditions will be able to use the Super Slot upon installing the patch.

We're adding various missions that you can complete by playing regularly. Clear them by the deadline to earn Donpa Tickets and Duel Medals. *You must be connected to the Internet to participate in Play Missions.

Exchange your Donpa Tickets and Duel Medals for auras, horns, decals, characters, titles, and Jukebox tracks at the new in-game Shop. We'll be updating the store lineup over time.

Free Matches* don't affect your rank, so feel free to jump in without any pressure.

*Head over to Ranked Match for the original World Match experience.

Matchmaking will now pit you against Rivals of similar skill level. Come out on top to earn bonus Donpa Tickets!

We've overhauled the main menu to make room for all the new modes. Now when you select World Match, Legend Competition, Ranked Match, and Free Match will show up as options.

All new Festivals will be 10 days instead of 3. There's more time to join the fun and rack up all of the Festival Point Rewards.

Alongside the extended Festivals, win streaks will now determine Festival Rankings rather than Festival Points. When a Festival is live, your longest win streak will appear on the leaderboard. If your team finishes in 2nd place, don't worry. Your win streak won't reset, allowing you to keep up your run.

AI Rival teams can now appear in your matches at random. Defeating them earns you bonus Festival Points!

Win even more crowns while playing Festivals!

Awarded to players who have a 5+ win streak.

These can be obtained once your Gadget Plate reaches Grand Master Plate or higher.

Previous Festival rewards added to the Shop

The following Gadgets, previously distributed as Festival rewards, can now be purchased* with Donpa Tickets from the Customize Gadgets screen.

*These can be purchased once your Gadget Plate reaches Master Plate or higher.

Super Slot added: Powering up the Gadget System

The Super Slot, the 7th Gadget slot, gives players even more ways to customize their racing strategy.

Alongside this addition, we've adjusted underpowered and overpowered Gadgets.

We've also introduced 1-slot variants of existing Gadgets that are compatible with the Super Slot.

To add more ways to drive, the update adds Mod Gadgets, which offer bigger stat bonuses than existing Tuner Gadgets, and the new Charge Gadgets.

Plus, we've adjusted the overall balance, shortening the time it takes Rings to spawn and buffing Acceleration Type Machines.

These changes will give racers in the middle of the pack chances to stage a comeback.

Going forward, more Gadget and Machine adjustments will be made based on usage and win rates.

Rings now take less time to respawn after players collect them.

In Ver. 1.4, it was difficult to collect Rings when racing alongside others. As a result, Gadgets that let players obtain Rings independently held a significant advantage.

We've implemented this change to shake up the meta, and give players in middle positions more chances for success.

Since these adjustments will make the Ring Engine Gadgets and Ring Evolution more powerful, we have rebalanced their performance accordingly.

*These adjustments do not apply to offline modes, such as Grand Prix and Race Park.

Shortened recovery time after taking damage.

Based on usage and win rates of Acceleration Type Machines, we have made adjustments to improve their signature trait of recovering quickly.

They should excel on courses with many enemies and obstacles, as well as in races where attacks are frequent.

Fixed an issue where Power Type Machines had a higher maximum speed bonus cap than other Machines.

Originally planned for Ver. 1.4.1, we postponed this fix to prevent an issue making it impossible to update your records in Time Trial. However, as the new Gadget Slot is likely to impact records in Ver. 2.0, we have proceeded with this change.

Adjusted Omochao's Ring placement so that Rings are easier to collect mid-jump.

While holding either Boost or Double Boost, the other item can now still spawn from an Item Box. Previously, holding either a Boost or Double Boost made both items less likely to appear.

Adjusted the explosion effect to better match the duration of its attack hitbox.

Adjusted the placement of Rings and Item Boxes to improve the risk-reward balance of certain paths on the following courses:

Since their introduction, Ring Engine and Hyper Ring Engine have maintained high win rates, particularly in Emerald Grade of Legend Competition

Since Ver. 2.0 makes it easier to maintain Rings due to the shortened Ring respawn times and the ability to equip an additional Gadget that grants Rings with the Super Slot, we've lowered the top speed bonus from these two Gadgets.

In parallel, we've adjusted Gadgets that make it easier to maintain your Rings:

Slipstream Bounty, Acceleration Character Kit, Slipstream Kit

The following Ring Gadgets have been enhanced. Since these Gadgets don't continuously collect Rings, these enhancements should have only a small impact on Ring Engine builds:

Increased the number of Rings you can receive from 15 to 25.

Increased the number of Rings you can receive from 4 to 6.

Held off on adjusting Mini Ring Thief due to its use in Ring Engine builds.

Ring Gain Boost/Acceleration Character Kit

The following Driving Gadgets were useful on certain courses and in certain situations, but in many cases ended up being underpowered We have enhanced their performance in Ver. 2.0 to make their unique abilities more distinct:

After a Perfect Landing, the duration of the maximum speed boost now increases proportionate to the number of Air Tricks performed.

Added an effect that makes all Levels charge 1.7x faster while in flight form.

Enhanced the Gadgets below to make them more useful in the current game environment:

Since balance adjustments can weaken Gadgets and make them less viable for setting new records in Time Trial, we may make separate Gadget adjustments for Time Trial alone starting in Ver. 2.0. For Ver. 2.0, the following Gadgets perform differently in Time Trial.

In Time Trial, reduced the top speed bonus for acquiring a Ring has been reduced from 3 km/h to 2 km/h.

*When equipped in the Super Slot, the bonus remains unchanged at 3 km/h.

In Time Trial, this Gadget will have the same performance as in Ver. 1.4. However, you will no longer get an additional stat boost by equipping both the Ring Engine and Hyper Ring Engine. You can get the same boost by equipping Quick Starter or Starting Boost Bounty as your 7th Gadget.

In Time Trial, this Gadget will have the same performance as in Ver. 1.4, and will evolve every 10 Rings.

In Time Trial, this Gadget will have the same performance as in Ver. 1.4.

#4098. Two Big Remasters Are Now Lined Up For Xbox On December 3rd

Including a first-ever Xbox appearance for the original Thief!

It's usually the case that December is a quiet time for new video game releases, but we've still got a few notable ones lined up for the first couple of weeks on Xbox, including two very interesting remasters on December 3rd.

We already knew about the first of these - Rayman Legends Retold is coming to Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S on that date. It seems a little bit redundant to "reimagine" an Xbox One game like Rayman Legends on the face of it, but the previews have been pretty great for the most part, and there's no doubt that Legends is a great game in general.

The next one has just been announced for December 3rd today though, and it's Thief: The Dark Project Remastered. The original Thief has never appeared on Xbox before, having first released on PC back in 1998, but it was considered one of the best games of that year across any platform, and has a whopping 92 average rating on Metacritic.

Its remaster is being handled by the experts at Nightdive Studios, known for an absolute ton of great remasters in recent years, so as long as you don't mind the dated nature of it, this could end up being a must-buy on the 3rd.

Exciting stuff! We'll leave you with more details on both games down below.

On this page: Two Big Remasters Are Now Lined Up For Xbox On December 3rd

Embark on a bold reimagining of the acclaimed platformer, filled with new content and narrative twists. When a shadowy villain spreads corruption across the Glade of Dreams, journey through its charming worlds solo or in up to 4‑player couch co‑op in a fast‑paced, side‑scrolling adventure where every stumble and surprise adds to the delightful chaos.

In Thief: The Dark Project Remastered, Nightdive Studios brings back the pioneering 3D stealth game from Looking Glass Studios. Described by its developers as a “first-person sneaker,” the 1998 title challenged norms with its non-confrontational gameplay at a time when most first-person games prioritized combat. Thief was the first stealth game to use light and sound as game mechanics to help you hide from and sneak up on characters, rather than simply attacking them. Remastered with Nightdive’s KEX Engine, the release includes Thief: The Dark Project and the additional missions, content and updates from the 1999 Thief Gold re-release.

#4097. HELENA : Cloud District is a megastructure photography game laser targeted at my interests, and it's out next week

Yes, I'm doing it, I'm writing about a megastructure game for the second time this week because come on, HELENA : Cloud District just looks stunning, don't it? Admittedly there's a chance you've not heard of it, that be the way of things in this algorithmically dominated world, but allow me to tell you about its big, scary world and the strange camera you're equipped with to capture all the sights it holds.

In the world of HELENA : Cloud District, you have come across a rotting megastructure that appears to be long abandoned, all sorts of strange flora dotted throughout it. In one part, it's something of a precision first-person platformer, as you navigate its intricately layered world with drops so steep you'd probably die before you hit the bottom. At the centre of it all is a computer, and it's here where you must bring all of your photographs in order to learn more about the history of the place.

The in-game camera itself is a fascinating thing to look at, completely impossible, alien and ancient in its design. From what I can tell it's a sort of metallic helmet, these insect-like segments snapping into place when you're gearing up to take a snap. You only appear to have three photo slots at any given point in time, meaning you can't just go gallivanting around the place all trigger happy like. There's an amount of care you have to put in positioning yourself and subsequently finding your way back to the central computer.

It's non-linear too, there's no set path you have to take, and it seems like there's some neat movement mechanics too. "Slide, hover, and glide through the structure in your own creative way in order to reach every level and get deeper into the slumbering Cloud District," explains the game's Steam page. Sounds like you don't have to worry too much about that falling to your death thing, then. I'm quite enthused by what HELENA : Cloud District is putting down, and it has a release date now too: October 29th. Same day as Hypnos! I now dub October 29th megastructure day. There will not be a vote on this matter. Ahead of HELENA's release, make sure to give it a wishlist on Steam.

#4096. "System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs. People called them RPGs": Gloomwood's publisher isn't too keen on using the term immersive sim despite it being one

You know, I think at this point in my life there is a non-zero chance I will die before anyone is able to settle comfortably on what defines an immersive sim. I'm not going to even try to! The idea is too annoying and I'm sure someone will disagree with some aspect of it. And if you ask New Blood boss Dave Oshry, when it comes to trying to flog an immersive sim, it's probably best to not even refer to it as one.

"Is it a good marketing term? No. It sucks," Oshry told PC Gamer in a recent interview. "It's awful." For those unfamiliar with New Blood, they're a publisher of some pretty cultishly popular games like ULTRAKILL, as well as immersive sims like Gloomwood and Fallen Aces. Ironically, though, it's through publishing Gloomwood and working with lead dev Dillon Rogers specifically that he even heard of the term. "He's like, 'That's what these are called'. I'm like, 'I have never heard that before in my life. What the fuck are you talking about?'"

That doesn't mean Oshry had never heard of or played an imsim before, he was familiar with classics like Deus Ex, he just considered them to be a different genre: RPGs. "System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs. People called them RPGs. That's the funny thing about an immersive sim. You're immersed in this world. You're building your character. Yeah, that's called an RPG, brother. That's a roleplaying game." Perhaps a controversial statement amongst the diehard imsim fans, but perhaps not an entirely untrue statement either.

In Oshry's opinion, "if you market something as an RPG, I think you'll do better than marketing it as an immersive sim." This part I'm not sure I'd entirely agree with. Sure, everyone knows what an RPG is, but they do also have certain expectations that come with them, such as stats and the like that you don't typically find in imsims. Ahah! Maybe that's the difference. Immersive sims are RPGs without the stats. By golly, I've done it without even trying. Either way, this Oshry fellow does seem to be pretty good at peddling weird little indies, so maybe I should just pipe down.

#4095. Sony Commits to China Hero Project with Further Investment into Promising PS5 Games

Many titles getting an additional $1 million

While the vast majority of its four million sales have no doubt been made on PC, Sony’s enjoying a big win with the console exclusive Phantom Blade Zero right now.

And at a press conference in Shanghai earlier today, it recommitted to its ongoing China Hero Project, which is now in its fourth phase.

As reported by Shenzhen-based journalist Daniel Camilo on X (or Twitter), the manufacturer has committed a further $1 million of investment to upcoming titles like EXILEDGE, DaBa: Land of Water Scar, and Unending Dawn.

Here’s how all three titles are described by Sony:

Daba: Land of Water Scar is a beautiful 'Souls-like' action adventure that tells the story of a puppet with a humanoid appearance exploring the ancient city of Guge during an imminent apocalypse. By doing battle with a range of horrific enemies he will unravel the story of both this ruined world, and himself.

A spectacular third-person shooter game featuring stunning visuals, a deep, emotional story and a rich cast of characters. Set on an apocalyptic planet, players will navigate the treacherous environment and face dangerous enemies in a series of thrilling missions.

Unending Dawn is a multiplayer open-world action game set in a world ravaged by a catastrophe where survivors struggle against cursed creatures. Embark on the Path of Cognition, confronting the dangers and unknowns of ancient legends to seek the truth - and a glimmer of hope.

Many of these games will launch on PC as well, although Sony will help promote them and bring them to a global audience in return for temporary console exclusivity.

Much like with Phantom Blade Zero, the Japanese giant’s goal appears to be attaching its brand to these titles, as it continues to grow its market share in China – a region primarily dominated by mobile and PC games.

As reported by Camilo, DaBa: Land of the Water Scar is due out in Spring 2027, although no official release date has been confirmed yet. Exiledge will follow later in the year.

These are just a handful of the titles Sony is currently working on, with Loulan: The Cursed Sand, The God Slayer, and more all also on the China Hero Project ledger.

I think this strategy is a multifaceted winner for Sony: not only does it help it infiltrate the huge Chinese market, but it’s also reaping dividends globally, where titles like Phantom Blade Zero are contributing to the PS5’s eclectic and diverse software mix.

#4094. Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen New Update & Anime Collab Announced, Here Are The Full Patch Notes

Capcom has this week announced a new update for its recent release Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen. It's already available on other platforms and will be live for the Switch 2 next week on 11th November 2026.

It comes loaded with added features and adjustments, and whole bunch of bug fixes, making updates to NPCs, the UI, Vocations, Pawns, Enemies and more. We'll provide an update when this is officially available on the Switch 2.

"The update for the Nintendo Switch 2 version is scheduled to release on November 11 PST / November 12 GMT. We apologize for the wait and appreciate your patience and understanding!"

In some other news, Capcom has also announced a new "Delicious in Dungeon" anime collab this week. It will include special pawns and outfit sets, and is available for a limited time. You can see the official trailer in the video above.

And here's the full rundown of the latest game update via Capcom's official Dragon's Dogma website:

◆ Added Features and AdjustmentsAdded Outfit Sets for Laios and Marcille from Delicious in Dungeon.

Availability: Until the January 28, 2027 Update Note: The Outfit Sets will be added to your storage after loading a saved data file during the period of availability.

If you haven't played Dragon's Dogma 2 (or its expansion Dark Arisen), be sure to check out our review. You can also download the game's character creator from the eShop.

#4093. Former Xbox COO Issues Lengthy Departure Statement To 'Set The Record Straight'

"This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end."

This time last week, we mentioned how newly-promoted Xbox Chief Operating Officer Helen Chiang was suddenly leaving Microsoft after 21 years, with a suggestion at the time that she may have been "terminated for policy violations".

Chiang has now taken to LinkedIn to share a lengthy departure statement in which she denies she was fired for a policy violation, but nevertheless suggests concerns regarding how certain things were handled in her case.

The statement does the talking for itself, so we'll share it in full down below:

"Clarity is Kindness There has been some speculation about my abrupt departure from Microsoft, including claims that I was “fired for a policy violation”. That’s not accurate and while I won’t turn this into a play-by-play, silence should not be mistaken for agreement. What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize. It’s important to me to set the record straight. First, I did not leak confidential company information to the press. I have never communicated with any journalist outside the limited, company-authorized interviews I’ve done as part of my job. That includes every journalist who reached out this week seeking my side of the story. Second, I did not leave XBOX to join a competitor. You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build. XBOX was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here. Third, I did not engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity. I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career. I won’t let speculation define my character or erase that record. Lastly, I did not leave because I was passed over for a bigger role. Since having children, I’ve been intentional about how I define ambition and success. I haven’t actively sought out bigger roles or increased responsibilities, and the last time I interviewed for a job was in 2011. My reputation and results paved the way for the opportunities that followed. I went where the company believed I was needed and where I could have the greatest impact. I did not ask for my most recent role, either. I was promoted into it in July. I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously. I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind. To everyone who has reached out with hugs, love, and support: thank you. So many of you have reminded me of the wonderful times we’ve shared over the past 20 years and the impact we’ve had on one another. Some of you I haven’t been in touch with for several years, yet you still took the time to check on me. Others are people I’ve never even met, but you reached out anyway. That speaks volumes about the care and humanity in our industry and the connections that transcend where we work. This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end. And it is not the whole story."

As you can see, Chiang starts her statement here with the phrase "clarity is kindness", which is a phrase that Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has used on numerous occasions since taking her role a few months ago.

Nothing specific is said about why Chiang was let go (or potentially decided to leave) as part of this statement though, and while she's certainly assertive in getting her point across, there's no evident malice directed at anyone.

Ultimately, she says she's publishing this statement to avoid being linked to "incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal", and that her story is about "staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard".

On behalf of everyone at Pure Xbox, we wish Chiang all the best in her future endeavours.

The best Rezi 12 builds in MW4 are all about doubling down on the classic strengths of a shotgun: namely the ability to end a foe with a single close-range blast, not bothering too much with accuracy and instead running around cutting through opponents. The Rezi 12 is currently the best shotgun in Modern Warfare 4, and if you make the right sort of build, you can turn it into an absolute killing machine.

For more info on deadly loadouts, check out our list of the best MW4 guns!

Though I've played with a few Rezi builds, this one remains easily the best one in my mind, one based around hipfiring with the Apex Enforcer mod, allowing for explosive slugs and pump-action cycling. This is a build for close-quarters encounters, moving rapidly, and hip-firing. The Heavy Silencer and Heavy Long Barrel are here to ensure maximum impact and effectively guarantee that any shot from the torso up will kill the opponents you encounter.

Meanwhile, the stock (or lack thereof), Assault Grip and Laser are all here to maximize hip fire accuracy and ease of use. This is a build where you fire the moment you see an enemy in close range, and works well as a secondary weapon in an assault loadout, with an AR as your primary.

#4091. Abelina is a strange, platforming romp through a natural afterlife from a former League of Legends animator and the composer of Zach Cregger's Resident Evil

Would that make what we're currently in the beforedeath?

I have no particular thoughts on what the afterlife may look like, namely because if there is one, and I'm allowed to hang out in it, I don't want to be disappointed. What if I have the expectation that it's a hedonistic paradise and am met with only having a guy named Gary who only eats cheese sandwiches for company? How embarrassing! No, I'll leave the imagining to others on this particular front. Doing so bears some ripe fruit for me occasionally, too, as is the case today with Abelina, a surreal platformer about a man who died and finds himself tending to gardens and carving masks and trying "not to think about what this place might really be."

My immediate reaction upon seeing Abelina is that it has the vibe of a Soviet stop motion film only Letterboxd users have heard of, which is perhaps the highest compliment I can give to a game graphically. In it, you play as Vasily, who "died a while ago." He finds himself in the titular Abelina, an odd, nature-filled afterlife, where he's been trying to find happiness again with a small handful of other folks doing the same.

I don't think Abelina is a puzzle game, but it does look like you have to put some thought into your platforming at points. There is flying to be done, dungbeetle-esque rolling, precise jumps to be made. It seems the entire thing is about navigating this otherworldly locale, and hopefully finding some truth amongst it all. You may not always find the correct path, with branching paths and open vistas seemingly offering a multitude of ways forward, all while being led by a "mysterious rabbit-cat."

It's also a game with some skill behind it, being led by Gabe Askew, who's worked on CG cinematics for the likes of Valorant, League of Legends and Love, Death + Robots. Sonically we should be in for a pleasant time too, as Weapons and the recent Resident Evil movie's composer Ryan Holladay is on the soundtrack for Abelina. I'm curious about what else it has to offer and am keen to get my hands on it to see how that platforming feels. In the meantime, you might join me by wishlisting it on Steam ahead of its release in 2027.

#4090. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are, again, for running taxi duty for relatives visiting from overseas. If I had a nickel for every time I had an early morning Gatwick run in tandem with a Sunday Papers post, I’d have two nickels, which isn’t a lot but it’s weird than I’m being paid in USD when I live in the United Kingdom. In that international spirit, here are some fine writings from around the globe.

For Stop Caring, Artemis Octavio interviewed Jeremy Couillard, the multimedia artist behind such offbeat indie experiments as Soul Injector Commando: an FPS about shooting a sense of humanity into enemies based on real-life billionaires.

This past week’s discourse on gamedev team sizes, sparked by a GI.biz post about Star Wars: Galactic Racer and its "core team" of 75, was clearly an inferior rehash of the Nic-sparked Expedition 33 one last year. But it has produced this thoughtful Game Developer piece, by Bryant Francis, on whether we need a new language approach to fit recent developments in outsourcing.

When done right, the model diversifies financial risk and preserves what works about triple-A development without the need to keep everyone under one corporate entity. When done wrong, you can wind up with a game development class system, where creative direction and funding flows in limited directions, and those not lucky enough to be at the center struggle to keep doing the work they love.

This problem is obviously organizational in nature, and not easily fixed by good copyediting. But organizations begin with language, and the language we use to define our work will define the future of video game development.

Writer and former Double Finer Harper Jay considers when games fail. In the interesting 'intent and aspirations' sense, not the tedious 'sales and Steam player counts' sense.

Manhunt’s investment into the stealth simulation is not insignificant, especially for the time. Even with the conceit that there is a snuff director engineering these scenarios, it wants you to understand that there is a world. It behaves largely as you might expect. The rules are mostly the rules of the real worlds. a brick falls because there is "gravity" and it makes "noise" like a normal brick would.

But! There’s rules to the game. Do X and a guard will do Y. Exploiting this is a key to progress and getting high scores. hit a wall, the mook says the thing, he walks over. this is the rule. at least so far.

But this guy doesn’t move. It’s not some meta-textual commentary, it’s not some undercutting trick on the player. He’s just not programmed that way. So I mention it to the game club. something’s up.

This doesn’t work. It doesn’t align. The simulation fails. The artifice is too obvious here. The funhouse is on display a bit too brazenly. It’s endearing maybe in the way that all jank can be. but it’s "off."

Eurogamer’s Robert Purchese meets the man who put a Game Boy Museum into a Game Boy cartridge.

I’ve been learning, as I recommend you do, about the eccentric American moneyman Timothy Dexter (1747-1806), whose preternatural luck in seeing his bumbling investments succeed was matched only by his zest for unhinged wordsmithing. Not really a 'from this week', of course. But then I only heard about the guy on Tuesday after Edwin, mad with fury after years of me editing commas into his articles, sent me Dexter’s punctuation sheet supplement, which he included in reprints of one work “Nowing ones complane of my book the fust edition had no stops”.

I did look around for something BioWare-related to include here, but to be perfectly honest I still think the best eulogy I've read is Edwin's. Even if the first draft needed some commas. Music this week is alternating between Clutch’s gigantic, dive-bombing Wasted Lands, and this SilvaGunner remix of Unbeatable’s best song. Good Sundays, all.

#4088. The First Review For Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Switch 2 Is In

It's a huge week in gaming with the highly anticipated launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2. The first review from the famous Japanese outlet Famitsu has now officially gone live. So, what did it think of Nintendo's remake?

If you aren't familiar with this publication's unique scoring system, four critics each deliver a score out of ten, and these scores are then totalled. For Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2, it's received 9/9/9/10, giving it an overall score of 37/40. So, it's been well received by the outlet!

In case you need a reminder, the original 1998 Nintendo 64 game was awarded a "perfect" score of 40/40. As for the 2011 3DS release, it was also given a score of 37/40. We'll be delivering our own final thoughts here on Nintendo Life later today, and be on the lookout for a review round up.

What's your reaction to this review score from Famitsu? Are you jumping into the remake this week? Tell us in the comments.
